On counterexamples to the Mertens conjecture

Seungki Kim Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Cincinnati, 4199 French Hall West, 2815 Commons Way, Cincinnati, OH 45221-0025, United States seungki.math@gmail.com  and  Phong Q. Nguyen Department of Computer Science, Ecole Normale Supérieure, 45 rue d’Ulm, 75005, Paris, France phong.nguyen@inria.fr
Abstract.

We use state-of-art lattice algorithms to improve the upper bound on the lowest counterexample to the Mertens conjecture to ≈exp⁡(1.96×1019)absent1.96superscript1019\approx\exp(1.96\times 10^{19})≈ roman_exp ( 1.96 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 19 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ), which is significantly below the conjectured value of ≈exp⁡(5.15×1023)absent5.15superscript1023\approx\exp(5.15\times 10^{23})≈ roman_exp ( 5.15 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 23 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ) by Kotnik and van de Lune [KvdL04].

1. Introduction

The Mertens conjecture [M97], dating back to 1897, is a statement about the growth rate of the Mertens function

M⁢(x):=∑1≤n≤xμ⁢(n),assign𝑀𝑥subscript1𝑛𝑥𝜇𝑛M(x):=\sum_{1\leq n\leq x}\mu(n),italic_M ( italic_x ) := ∑ start_POSTSUBSCRIPT 1 ≤ italic_n ≤ italic_x end_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_μ ( italic_n ) ,

where μ⁢(n)𝜇𝑛\mu(n)italic_μ ( italic_n ) is the Möbius function

μ⁢(n)={(−1)kif n is squarefree, and has k distinct prime factors,0if n is not squarefree.𝜇𝑛casessuperscript1𝑘if n is squarefree, and has k distinct prime factors,0if n is not squarefree.\mu(n)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{k}&\mbox{if $n$ is squarefree, and has $k$ distinct % prime factors,}\\ 0&\mbox{if $n$ is not squarefree.}\end{cases}italic_μ ( italic_n ) = { start_ROW start_CELL ( - 1 ) start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT italic_k end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT end_CELL start_CELL if italic_n is squarefree, and has italic_k distinct prime factors, end_CELL end_ROW start_ROW start_CELL 0 end_CELL start_CELL if italic_n is not squarefree. end_CELL end_ROW

The size of M⁢(x)𝑀𝑥M(x)italic_M ( italic_x ) is of interest in number theory, since it is closely related to the size of the real parts of the zeroes of the Riemann zeta function ζ⁢(s)𝜁𝑠\zeta(s)italic_ζ ( italic_s ). For example, a short argument (See e.g. [OtR85, Sec. 2]) shows that if M⁢(x)=O⁢(xθ)𝑀𝑥𝑂superscript𝑥𝜃M(x)=O(x^{\theta})italic_M ( italic_x ) = italic_O ( italic_x start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT italic_θ end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ), then the Riemann zeta function ζ⁢(s)𝜁𝑠\zeta(s)italic_ζ ( italic_s ) has no zeroes on the half-plane Re⁢s>θRe𝑠𝜃\mathrm{Re}\,s>\thetaroman_Re italic_s > italic_θ. For θ=1/2+ε𝜃12𝜀\theta=1/2+\varepsilonitalic_θ = 1 / 2 + italic_ε for arbitrarily small ε>0𝜀0\varepsilon>0italic_ε > 0, the latter statement is the famous Riemann hypothesis. The Mertens conjecture is a much bolder claim that

(1.1) |M⁢(x)|⁢<x1/2⁢ for all ⁢x>⁢1.𝑀𝑥expectationsuperscript𝑥12 for all 𝑥1|M(x)|<x^{1/2}\mbox{ for all }x>1.| italic_M ( italic_x ) | < italic_x start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 1 / 2 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT for all italic_x > 1 .

It took nearly a century for this conjecture to be disproved, by Odlyzko and te Riele [OtR85] in 1985. Their argument consisted of certain insights from classical analytic number theory, and, perhaps surprisingly, the use of a lattice reduction algorithm. No alternative (dis)proof that does not rely on lattice reduction is known to this day.

A natural follow-up is to ask about the size of the smallest counterexample 𝔵𝔵\mathfrak{x}fraktur_x to the Mertens conjecture (1.1). This is also related to the estimation of the growth rate of M⁢(x)𝑀𝑥M(x)italic_M ( italic_x ), for which several different conjectures exist. For example, the experimental work by Kotnik and van de Lune [KvdL04] suggests that

(1.2) |M⁢(x)⁢x−1/2|≈1/2⋅log⁡log⁡log⁡x𝑀𝑥superscript𝑥12⋅12𝑥|M(x)x^{-1/2}|\approx 1/2\cdot\sqrt{\log\log\log x}| italic_M ( italic_x ) italic_x start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT - 1 / 2 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT | ≈ 1 / 2 ⋅ square-root start_ARG roman_log roman_log roman_log italic_x end_ARG

along the local extrema of M⁢(x)/x1/2𝑀𝑥superscript𝑥12M(x)/x^{1/2}italic_M ( italic_x ) / italic_x start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 1 / 2 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT, from which they derive the conjecture that

(1.3) 𝔵≈exp⁡(5.15×1023),𝔵5.15superscript1023\mathfrak{x}\approx\exp(5.15\times 10^{23}),fraktur_x ≈ roman_exp ( 5.15 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 23 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ) ,

since 1/2⋅log⁡log⁡(5.15×1023)≈1⋅125.15superscript102311/2\cdot\sqrt{\log\log(5.15\times 10^{23})}\approx 11 / 2 ⋅ square-root start_ARG roman_log roman_log ( 5.15 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 23 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ) end_ARG ≈ 1.

It is also possible to give rigorous upper bounds on 𝔵𝔵\mathfrak{x}fraktur_x, thanks to Pintz [P87]. The original data of Odlyzko and te Riele [OtR85], under the theorem of Pintz [P87], translates to the statement that 𝔵<exp⁡(3.21×1064)𝔵3.21superscript1064\mathfrak{x}<\exp(3.21\times 10^{64})fraktur_x < roman_exp ( 3.21 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 64 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ). The later more extensive set of experiments by Kotnik and te Riele [KtR06] led to the improvement 𝔵<exp⁡(1.59×1040)𝔵1.59superscript1040\mathfrak{x}<\exp(1.59\times 10^{40})fraktur_x < roman_exp ( 1.59 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 40 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ). Saouter and te Riele [StR14] refined the estimates given in [P87], and also ran more experiments of the same kind, which resulted in 𝔵<exp⁡(1.004×1033)𝔵1.004superscript1033\mathfrak{x}<\exp(1.004\times 10^{33})fraktur_x < roman_exp ( 1.004 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 33 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ).

[OtR85] states that their achievement was possible thanks to a then-breakthrough in lattice reduction, the LLL algorithm due to Lenstra, Lenstra, and Lovász [LLL82]. [KtR06] and [StR14] also used LLL, and so did the relatively recent works such as Hurst [H18, Theorem 6.1]. However, over the last decade, there has been a huge amount of progress in lattice reduction techniques — largely motivated by the emergence of post-quantum cryptography based on computationally hard lattice problems. Noticing this, one would naturally be inclined to apply them to the context of the Mertens conjecture. Kim and Rozmarynowycz [KR23] was the first to point this out and to partially implement this idea, by simply replacing LLL with the BKZ algorithm ([SE94], [CN11]). As a result, they obtained a further improvement that 𝔵<exp⁡(1.017×1029)𝔵1.017superscript1029\mathfrak{x}<\exp(1.017\times 10^{29})fraktur_x < roman_exp ( 1.017 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 29 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ). [KR23] was, however, still far from taking the full advantage of the recent advances in lattice problems.

In this work, we employ state-of-art lattice point enumeration techniques [LN13, GNR10] in search of a tighter upper bound on the lowest counterexample to the Mertens conjecture (1.1). As explained in Section 3 below, this is a much more natural and efficient strategy than running lattice reduction hundreds to thousands of times, which has been the method chosen by all the previous works mentioned above. We also give a careful consideration to the family of the lattices under question, since such an understanding is important for both predicting the outcome and improving the performance of the algorithm. As a result, we improve the choice of the lattice made by [OtR85] in a couple of ways, for the first time in the past 38 years. Moreover, we notice that our lattices are extremely orthogonal, with one unusually short vector; we adapt the enumeration algorithm accordingly to exploit this special shape, effectively speeding up our search by a factor of a few millions.

Thereby we were able to find a number of data points that beat the previous record and even the conjecture (1.3) by several orders of magnitude. The best we found, which took us barely half a day on a single core, implies that

(1.4) 𝔵<exp⁡(1.96×1019),𝔵1.96superscript1019\mathfrak{x}<\exp(1.96\times 10^{19}),fraktur_x < roman_exp ( 1.96 × 10 start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT 19 end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ) ,

which is below (1.3) by a factor of ≈26276absent26276\approx 26276≈ 26276 in the exponent. This would substantially impact the credibility of (1.2). A more extensive application of the methods of the present paper may help search for an alternative estimate on the growth rate of M⁢(x)𝑀𝑥M(x)italic_M ( italic_x ) — see Section 4.2 below.

There exist also numerous other applications of the computational aspect of lattices to number theory than the Mertens conjecture, see e.g. Simon [S10]. We hope that our work helps inform the community of the recent advances in lattice computations, and encourages revisiting some of the old problems with the new arsenal.

Organization

In Section 2, we briefly review the method of Odlyzko-te Riele [OtR85] and other works in the literature, in order to help the reader understand and put our work into perspective. In Section 3, we describe our experiment in detail. We conclude the paper in Section 4 with a discussion on further research directions to which the methods introduced herein may be applied.

Reproducibility

The present work involves significant data. Data files and/or source codes allowing to reproduce the data are available on https://zenodo.org/records/10775723.

Given a basis of a lattice such as this one, lattice reduction algorithms such as LLL compute another basis of the same lattice consisting of vectors of reasonably short length (depending on the strength of the algorithm), called a reduced basis of that lattice.

3. Our experiment

3.1. Lattice point enumeration

The method of lattice reduction for finding y𝑦yitalic_y satisfying the conditions of Theorem 2.1 has a few limitations. To maximize (2.6) or (2.7), it makes sense to account for as many summands as possible, that is, to take N𝑁Nitalic_N as large as possible. However, high-quality lattice reduction becomes extremely time-consuming for N≥100𝑁100N\geq 100italic_N ≥ 100, so the trial-and-error strategy of [KR23] would take too much computational resource: non-trivial lattice tasks such as finding a closest lattice point typically run in time exponential in N𝑁Nitalic_N. Furthermore, maximizing (2.6) or (2.7) is not exactly a lattice problem: it is possible that the optimal solution does not arise from a particularly close lattice point. The terms on the right-hand side of (2.6) or (2.7) that are left out in the construction (2.3) turn out to be large enough to affect the outcome either in or against our favor, and they are essentially the matter of a coin toss.

The technique of lattice point enumeration provides a natural solution to this dilemma. When the lattice dimension is moderate, it is possible to enumerate all the lattice points within any small ball, or if the ball is larger, to enumerate many lattice points inside the ball. To do this, a standard algorithm is enumeration with pruning [LN13, GNR10], building upon work by Pohst [P81], Kannan [K83], and Schnorr-Euchner [SE94]. Gama, Nguyen and Regev [GNR10] showed how to speed up rigorously the Schnorr-Euchner [SE94] enumeration of lattice points within a zero-centered ball, which consists of a depth-first search (DFS) of a carefully constructed tree. This technique was later adapted to any ball by Liu and Nguyen [LN13].

Moving onto another topic, let us perform a small “sanity check” on our overall approach. When one transforms the problem of maximizing |hP|subscriptℎ𝑃|h_{P}|| italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_P end_POSTSUBSCRIPT | or |hS⁢t⁢R|subscriptℎ𝑆𝑡𝑅|h_{StR}|| italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_S italic_t italic_R end_POSTSUBSCRIPT | into a lattice problem, one makes several approximations, as discussed in the above sections. We would like to retrospectively check how sound these approximations are.

First, instead of considering the whole sum, we focus on the partial sum with the largest weights αi∗superscriptsubscript𝛼𝑖\alpha_{i}^{*}italic_α start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i end_POSTSUBSCRIPT start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT ∗ end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT: Figure 2 shows the correlations between hS⁢t⁢Rsubscriptℎ𝑆𝑡𝑅h_{StR}italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_S italic_t italic_R end_POSTSUBSCRIPT and its value when restricted to the terms corresponding to the lattice. This confirms that high (resp. low) values of hS⁢t⁢Rsubscriptℎ𝑆𝑡𝑅h_{StR}italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_S italic_t italic_R end_POSTSUBSCRIPT are indeed found among high (resp. low) values of the partial sum.

Second, when searching for high (resp. low) values of the partial sum, we enumerate a large number of lattice points close to some target. Figure 3 displays hS⁢t⁢R⁢(y)subscriptℎ𝑆𝑡𝑅𝑦h_{StR}(y)italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_S italic_t italic_R end_POSTSUBSCRIPT ( italic_y ) depending on the distance between the target and the lattice point: we see that the values maximizing hS⁢t⁢R⁢(y)subscriptℎ𝑆𝑡𝑅𝑦h_{StR}(y)italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_S italic_t italic_R end_POSTSUBSCRIPT ( italic_y ) are not necessarily those minimizing the distance, but hP⁢(y)>1subscriptℎ𝑃𝑦1h_{P}(y)>1italic_h start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_P end_POSTSUBSCRIPT ( italic_y ) > 1 looks unlikely to occur when the distance is bigger than some threshold. This means that we should enumerate a ball, but not a too large ball.

4. Further research topics

4.1. More improvement on the lowest counterexample

It seems plausible to us that, upon more extensive experiments and considerations, an even lower bound than our result (1.4) may be attainable. For instance, the choice of the parameters could be improved. The heuristics (3.6) and (3.7) suggest that perhaps one should increase ν𝜈\nuitalic_ν considerably. However, one must also be conscious of the effect of such maneuver on the shape of the lattice (3.2). If ν𝜈\nuitalic_ν is large, then νysubscript𝜈𝑦\nu_{y}italic_ν start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_y end_POSTSUBSCRIPT must be of comparable size to ν𝜈\nuitalic_ν, in order for the exponent of 2222 in (3.7) to fall within a reasonable range. Hence, it may no longer be the case that ν≫νymuch-greater-than𝜈subscript𝜈𝑦\nu\gg\nu_{y}italic_ν ≫ italic_ν start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_y end_POSTSUBSCRIPT, which was a crucial condition for the efficiency of our approach. There may be a “sweet spot” choice of parameters balancing these and other factors to be taken into account, but it is currently unclear to us as to how to determine them, other than by trial and error.

A further improvement on the theoretical side may also lead to a better bound. Recently, Hathi [H23, Sec. 2.2] refined some of the crucial estimates given by [StR14], but it appears that he did not exploit it to the full extent.

4.3. Linear relations among the zeroes of ζ⁢(s)𝜁𝑠\zeta(s)italic_ζ ( italic_s )

Best and Trudgian [BT15] presented a remarkable alternative proof to the Mertens conjecture, along the lines of the idea first suggested by Ingham [I42]. According to [I42], if the Mertens conjecture were true, there would exist infinitely many linear relations of the form

(4.2) ∑i=1Nci⁢γi=0,ci∈ℤ⁢ not all zero,formulae-sequencesuperscriptsubscript𝑖1𝑁subscript𝑐𝑖subscript𝛾𝑖0subscript𝑐𝑖ℤ not all zero,\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}\gamma_{i}=0,c_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}\mbox{ not all zero,}∑ start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i = 1 end_POSTSUBSCRIPT start_POSTSUPERSCRIPT italic_N end_POSTSUPERSCRIPT italic_c start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i end_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_γ start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i end_POSTSUBSCRIPT = 0 , italic_c start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i end_POSTSUBSCRIPT ∈ blackboard_Z not all zero,

among the imaginary values of the zeroes of ζ⁢(s)𝜁𝑠\zeta(s)italic_ζ ( italic_s ). Later efforts weakened the condition (4.2) to the existence of one such relation with bounded N𝑁Nitalic_N and cisubscript𝑐𝑖c_{i}italic_c start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i end_POSTSUBSCRIPT’s — see [BT15, Theorem 2], attributed to Anderson and Stark. Using the LLL algorithm differently from [OtR85], [BT15] was able to prove the nonexistence of such a relation, the associated lattice problem being to find a nearly orthogonal basis of a given lattice. The reduced basis they found implies in particular that (4.2) is false for N=500𝑁500N=500italic_N = 500 and |ci|≤4976subscript𝑐𝑖4976|c_{i}|\leq 4976| italic_c start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_i end_POSTSUBSCRIPT | ≤ 4976, and that lim supx→∞|q⁢(x)|≥1.6383subscriptlimit-supremum→𝑥𝑞𝑥1.6383\limsup_{x\rightarrow\infty}|q(x)|\geq 1.6383lim sup start_POSTSUBSCRIPT italic_x → ∞ end_POSTSUBSCRIPT | italic_q ( italic_x ) | ≥ 1.6383. It would be natural to apply the advanced toolkits on lattice problems available today to improve on these numbers.

It is widely believed that relations of the form (4.2) do not exist. This statement is called the linear independence conjecture, and has far-reaching consequences in number theory — see [N04] and the references therein for details.
